14i5ei9:310: Levie uses Gell-Mann amnesia to explain outsiders' overestimation: when people use their own AI, they see the trivial finishing work and context; when looking at others' work, they only see the "first 80%" textual output. The truly hard-to-automate part is exactly the final 20%—asking the right questions, filling in missing information, reviewing outputs, responding to security incidents, and ensuring system launch and quality. More critical is the dynamic equation: after automating the first 90%, the market immediately raises expectations, turning 90% into a new 50%, so demand growth continuously offsets capability substitution. This explains the "If You Give a Mouse a Cookie" effect—AI lowers the fixed cost of starting a task, making things that were previously not worth doing feasible, and in turn creates more downstream work, even spawning new roles (Levie jokes about considering hiring a dedicated person to accompany him on agent customer research).
